Freshwater says schools can act as neutral brokers as geopolitical tension tests global research Universities must work more closely with industry, business and government to turn research into real-world impact, and Korean universities are well placed to do so as the country’s research standing rises, according to the head of a global university alliance.
Dawn Freshwater, executive director of the Worldwide Universities Network (WUN), made the remarks in an interview with The Korea Times Thursday, during the Times Higher Education Innovation & Impact Summit 2026 at Korea University in Seoul. WUN is a consortium of research-intensive universities across six continents that funds and supports international research collaboration among its members.
Freshwater said universities have long been cut off from government, industry and business. They have tried to produce graduates who are ready for work, she said, but their research has not always done as much to advance society and industry.
“The fourth generation of university is now teaching, research and innovation for societal impact,” she said, describing how universities moved from teaching alone, to teaching and research, then to innovation and now to delivering benefits for society. A fourth-generation university acts as a driver of regional innovation, combining education, research and innovation to solve real-world social and economic problems.
To make that shift, she said, universities need strong ties with industry, business and government. They can also learn from how institutions in other countries work with technology institutes and businesses to raise the economic value of a university education.
Asked how visible Korean universities are in global research networks, Freshwater said it is “all relative.” It is very difficult to match the scale of research and development spending in the United States, where much of the money comes from large companies, philanthropists and alumni.
“But I actually think Korea is really on an upward trajectory from a research point of view,” she said, citing the high quality of Korean students and talent.
She said her former schools had worked with Korean partners, pointing to Korea University’s Climate Corps program. Through the program, foreign students join Korean students in climate-related activities and learn about research and graduate study opportunities in Korea.
On geopolitical tension, Freshwater said universities mostly stay neutral, which lets them run cross-border projects across disciplines, such as cancer research that is now aiming for cures rather than only treatment.
She acknowledged that governments take different positions on data sovereignty, meaning national control over where data is stored and how it is shared. Universities therefore need to work closely with governments to understand national priorities and limits.
“This is not the first time that we’ve been in difficult geopolitical contexts, and we’ve navigated our way through it,” she said, adding that higher education can serve as a broker of knowledge and a channel for soft diplomacy.
